subject: Geography
unitTitle: Major Geological Processes Associated with Plate Tectonics

questions.question: Which German meteorologist proposed the Continental Drift Theory in 1912, hypothesizing that all present continents were once joined in a single supercontinent called Pangaea?
questions.explanation: Alfred Wegener proposed the Continental Drift Theory in 1912, suggesting that all modern continents originally formed a single massive supercontinent named Pangaea ('all-Earth') surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean.

questions.question: According to Plate Tectonics Theory, across which semi-fluid, ductile layer of the upper mantle do rigid tectonic lithospheric plates slide?
questions.explanation: The Earth's lithosphere (crust and uppermost solid mantle) floats and slowly slides across the underlying asthenosphere, a hot, semi-fluid layer of the upper mantle capable of plastic flow.

questions.question: What type of tectonic plate boundary occurs where two plates pull apart from each other, allowing magma to upwell and create new oceanic crust?
questions.explanation: Divergent or constructive boundaries occur where plates move in opposite directions away from each other. As they separate, molten mantle material rises to fill the gap, creating new oceanic lithosphere at mid-ocean ridges.

questions.question: Which major earthquake and volcanic belt encircles the Pacific Ocean basin, accounting for approximately 80% of all global seismic energy release?
questions.explanation: The Circum-Pacific Belt, popularly known as the 'Ring of Fire,' borders the mountainous coastlines and island arcs surrounding the Pacific Ocean, where roughly 80% of global earthquake energy and active volcanism occur.

questions.question: Which of the following processes is classified as an endogenic (internal) geological force operating beneath or within the Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Endogenic forces originate within the Earth's interior (such as plate tectonics, folding, faulting, and volcanic eruptions). In contrast, wind, running water, and glaciers are exogenic (external) forces operating on the surface.

questions.question: What was the primary scientific objection that caused Alfred Wegener's Continental Drift Theory to be rejected by geologists in the 1920s?

options.text: Fossil evidence matching across separate continents was proven to be fabricated.
He could not explain a plausible physical mechanism capable of moving heavy continental landmasses across the solid sea floor.
Direct satellite GPS measurements proved continents were completely stationary.
The matching coastline geometries of South America and Africa were disproven by hydrographic mapping.

questions.explanation: Although Wegener presented compelling geological and paleontological evidence, he could not explain the physical mechanism responsible for moving continents (incorrectly proposing tidal forces or centrifugal force), leading to the rejection of his theory until sea-floor spreading was discovered in the 1960s.

questions.question: When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate at a convergent boundary, why does the oceanic plate subduct beneath the continental plate into the asthenosphere?

options.text: Oceanic crust is thicker and warmer than continental crust.
Oceanic crust (composed of basalt) is significantly denser and heavier than continental crust (composed of granite).
Continental crust moves at a higher horizontal velocity than oceanic crust.
Geomagnetic polarity pulls oceanic crust downward into the outer core.

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is composed of basaltic rocks with a high density (~3.0 g/cm³), making it heavier than continental crust made of granitic rocks (~2.7 g/cm³). During collision, the denser oceanic plate is forced downward (subducted) into the mantle below the lighter continental plate.

questions.question: What landform feature is created when crustal tension causes a central block of rock to sink downward between two roughly parallel normal fault lines?
questions.explanation: Parallel faulting under tensional stress causes the central land block between two fault lines to displace downward relative to side blocks, forming an elongated fault trough called a graben or rift valley. The raised side blocks form horsts.

questions.question: The ongoing collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate at a continental-continental convergent boundary resulted in the formation of which major young fold mountain system?
questions.explanation: The Himalayas were formed by continental-continental collision when the northward-drifting Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate, compressing sediments of the ancient Tethys Sea into massive elevated mountain folds.

questions.question: Which driving force of plate motion occurs as a cold, dense subducting oceanic lithospheric slab sinks into the asthenosphere, pulling the rest of the trailing plate along behind it?
questions.explanation: Slab pull is the primary gravitational driving force of plate motion where a cold, dense subducting oceanic plate sinks into the warmer, less dense mantle at subduction zones, dragging the trailing plate behind it.

questions.question: Which depositional landform features characteristically develop in the lower course of a river where gradient flattens and water flow velocity drops significantly?
questions.explanation: In its lower course, a river flows slowly over flat terrain, losing kinetic energy. It deposits suspended alluvial materials to form flat, expansive floodplains, natural levees, and deltas near its outlet.

questions.question: Late Paleozoic glacial striations and tillite deposits of identical age (Carboniferous-Permian) are found across Southern Africa, South America, India, Australia, and Antarctica. How does this paleoclimatic evidence support Continental Drift Theory?

options.text: It proves that equatorial regions experienced global sub-zero atmospheric cooling during the Permian period.
It demonstrates that these now widely separated southern landmasses were contiguous and located near the South Pole as part of Gondwanaland before drifting apart.
It indicates that ancient oceans flooded all continents up to an altitude of 4,000 meters.
It shows that massive volcanic ash clouds blocked solar radiation across the entire Northern Hemisphere.

questions.explanation: Glacial striations and tillite deposits of Carboniferous-Permian age in tropical/subtropical regions like India, Brazil, and Southern Africa cannot be explained by localized weather. They indicate that these landmasses were merged near the South Pole into the supercontinent Gondwana, sharing a single ice cap before drifting to their present positions.

questions.question: The Afar Depression in the Horn of Africa is a world-renowned geological example of a 'triple junction.' Which three tectonic plates meet and diverge at this rifting center?

options.text: Eurasian Plate, Anatolian Plate, and African Plate
Nubian (African) Plate, Somali Plate, and Arabian Plate
Indian Plate, Australian Plate, and Antarctic Plate
Nazca Plate, Cocos Plate, and South American Plate

questions.explanation: The Afar Triple Junction is an active tectonic boundary where three spreading rifts meet: the Nubian (African Main) Plate, the Somali Plate, and the Arabian Plate, forming the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and East African Rift arms.

questions.question: How does an earthquake's 'focus' (hypocenter) differ structurally from its 'epicenter', and how do Primary (P) waves and Secondary (S) waves behave during propagation?

options.text: Focus is the surface location; epicenter is the underground origin point. S-waves arrive before P-waves.

Focus is the underground origin point where fault rupture begins; epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly vertically above the focus. P-waves travel faster and pass through solids and liquids, while S-waves are slower and pass only through solids.
Focus is measured on the Richter scale; epicenter is measured on the Mercalli scale. P-waves pass only through liquids.
Focus occurs only in oceanic trenches; epicenter occurs only on block mountains. P-waves and S-waves travel at identical velocities.

questions.explanation: The focus (hypocenter) is the underground point within the crust where energy release and fault movement originate. The epicenter is the position on the Earth's surface directly above the focus. Compressional P-waves are the fastest seismic waves and travel through both solids and liquids, whereas transverse S-waves are slower and cannot propagate through fluids.

questions.question: Which intrusive igneous body forms when magma forces its way vertically or near-vertically across pre-existing rock strata (discordant) and solidifies into a wall-like underground sheet?
questions.explanation: A dike is a discordant igneous intrusion formed when magma cuts vertically or steeply across bedding planes of existing rock strata. A sill is a concordant horizontal sheet intruded parallel to rock layers, while a batholith is a vast underground plutonic mass.
